### Later years, health problems and death
[edit]
As early as 1952, when _The Jackie Gleason Show_ captured Saturday night for CBS, Gleason regularly smoked six packs of cigarettes a day.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-66)
Gleason struggled with weight issues throughout much of his life, often weighing close to 300 pounds. His diet primarily consisted of red meat and rich desserts, with little to no vegetables. Additionally, Gleason did not engage in regular exercise and consumed alcohol excessively.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-67)
In _The Golden Ham: A Candid Biography of Jackie Gleason_, author Jim Bishop notes that Gleason had three separate wardrobes to accommodate his fluctuating weight, which varied between 185 and 285 pounds.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-68)
Gleason's sarcophagus—with the inscription "And Away We Go"—at Our Lady of Mercy Catholic Cemetery in Miami
In 1978 he suffered chest pains while touring in the lead role of Larry Gelbart's play _Sly Fox_ and later underwent triple-bypass surgery.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-surgery-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-71)
texts.30:
### Later years, health problems and death
Gleason delivered a critically acclaimed performance as an infirm, acerbic, and somewhat Archie Bunker-like character in the Tom Hanks comedy-drama _Nothing in Common_ (1986), Gleason's final film role. During production he was diagnosed with colon cancer, which had metastasized to his liver. He was also suffering from phlebitis and diabetes. He kept his medical problems private, although there were rumors that he was seriously ill.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-72) On June 24, 1987, he died at age 71 in his Florida home.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-73)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-Pace_nytimes-10)
After a funeral mass at the Cathedral of Saint Mary, Gleason was entombed in a sarcophagus in a private outdoor mausoleum at Our Lady of Mercy Catholic Cemetery in Miami.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-Obit-64) Gleason's sister-in-law June Taylor is buried to the left of the mausoleum, next to her husband and attorney, Sol Lerner.

### Later years, health problems and death
*   A 1978 Lincoln Continental limousine, formerly owned by Jackie Gleason, was featured on the TV show "Pawn Stars". The episode, titled "To The Moon," showcased the car when a seller brought it into the Gold & Silver Pawn Shop. The car was a highlight, with Rick Harrison expressing interest due to its celebrity provenance. Ultimately, the car's condition and the expert's assessment determined its fate on the show.  
*   Miami Beach in 1987 renamed the Miami Beach Auditorium as the Jackie Gleason Theater of the Performing Arts. As of May 2010, the theater was scheduled to be razed as part of a convention center remodeling project and replaced by a hotel.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-75) The demolition did not take place and The Fillmore Miami Beach is still in operation as of January 2024.  
*   Gleason was inducted into the Academy of Television Arts & SciencesTelevision Hall of Fame in 1986.  
*   In 2000 a statue of him as Ralph Kramden in "And away we go!" pose was installed at the Miami Beach Bus Terminal.  
*   Gleason was nominated three times for an Emmy Award, but never won. (Carney and Kean did, however.)  
*   In 1976 at the Sixth Annual American Guild of Variety Artists (AGVA) "Entertainer of the Year Awards", Paul Lynde received an award for being voted the funniest man of the year.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-76) Lynde immediately turned his award over to host Jackie Gleason, citing him as "the funniest man ever." The unexpected gesture shocked Gleason.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-77)
texts.32:
### Later years, health problems and death
*   On June 30, 1988, the Sunset ParkMTA, NYCT's 5th Avenue Bus Depot in Brooklyn was renamed the Jackie Gleason Depot in honor of the native Brooklynite.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-78)  
*   A statue of Gleason as Ralph Kramden in his bus driver's uniform was dedicated in August 2000 in New York City in Manhattan at the 40th Street entrance of the Port Authority Bus Terminal (PABT). The statue was briefly shown in the film _World Trade Center_ (2006).  
*   A city park in Lauderhill, Florida, was named the "Jackie Gleason Park" in his honor; it is located near his former home and features racquetball and basketball courts and a children's playground.  
*   Signs on the Brooklyn Bridge which advise drivers that they are entering Brooklyn have the Gleason phrase "How Sweet It Is!"  
*   Late in his life actor-playwright Jason Miller, Gleason's former son-in-law, was writing a screenplay based on Gleason's life. He died before it was completed.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-Linda-52)  
*   Gleason was portrayed by Brad Garrett in a 2002 television biopic about his life.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-80)

# The History
## AN INNOVATIVE HISTORY
Inspired by a bold vision and deep respect for the land, Babcock Ranch’s creation was led by Syd Kitson, Chairman and CEO of Kitson & Partners, to become America’s first solar-powered town.
Honoring the heritage of Southwest Florida while embracing innovation, its founding enabled the largest preservation land purchase in Florida’s history and the creation of the 73,000-acre Babcock Ranch Preserve.

# The History
## AN INSPIRED VISION
Today, half of the town’s 18,000 acres are dedicated to greenways, parks, and lakes. From water-conserving landscapes to energy-efficient homes and solar fields that produce more clean power than the town consumes, every element reflects a pioneering model of sustainable living — one that respects the past while building a resilient future.

### Later years, health problems and death
[edit]
As early as 1952, when _The Jackie Gleason Show_ captured Saturday night for CBS, Gleason regularly smoked six packs of cigarettes a day.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-66)
Gleason struggled with weight issues throughout much of his life, often weighing close to 300 pounds. His diet primarily consisted of red meat and rich desserts, with little to no vegetables. Additionally, Gleason did not engage in regular exercise and consumed alcohol excessively.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-67)
In _The Golden Ham: A Candid Biography of Jackie Gleason_, author Jim Bishop notes that Gleason had three separate wardrobes to accommodate his fluctuating weight, which varied between 185 and 285 pounds.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-68)
Gleason's sarcophagus—with the inscription "And Away We Go"—at Our Lady of Mercy Catholic Cemetery in Miami
In 1978 he suffered chest pains while touring in the lead role of Larry Gelbart's play _Sly Fox_ and later underwent triple-bypass surgery.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-surgery-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-71)

### Later years, health problems and death
Gleason delivered a critically acclaimed performance as an infirm, acerbic, and somewhat Archie Bunker-like character in the Tom Hanks comedy-drama _Nothing in Common_ (1986), Gleason's final film role. During production he was diagnosed with colon cancer, which had metastasized to his liver. He was also suffering from phlebitis and diabetes. He kept his medical problems private, although there were rumors that he was seriously ill.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-72) On June 24, 1987, he died at age 71 in his Florida home.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-73)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-Pace_nytimes-10)
After a funeral mass at the Cathedral of Saint Mary, Gleason was entombed in a sarcophagus in a private outdoor mausoleum at Our Lady of Mercy Catholic Cemetery in Miami.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-Obit-64) Gleason's sister-in-law June Taylor is buried to the left of the mausoleum, next to her husband and attorney, Sol Lerner.
Ralph Kramden statue at the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Manhattan

The television home of _The Honeymooners_ at 328 Chauncey Street in Brooklyn

### Later years, health problems and death
*   A 1978 Lincoln Continental limousine, formerly owned by Jackie Gleason, was featured on the TV show "Pawn Stars". The episode, titled "To The Moon," showcased the car when a seller brought it into the Gold & Silver Pawn Shop. The car was a highlight, with Rick Harrison expressing interest due to its celebrity provenance. Ultimately, the car's condition and the expert's assessment determined its fate on the show.  
*   Miami Beach in 1987 renamed the Miami Beach Auditorium as the Jackie Gleason Theater of the Performing Arts. As of May 2010, the theater was scheduled to be razed as part of a convention center remodeling project and replaced by a hotel.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-75) The demolition did not take place and The Fillmore Miami Beach is still in operation as of January 2024.  
*   Gleason was inducted into the Academy of Television Arts & SciencesTelevision Hall of Fame in 1986.  
*   In 2000 a statue of him as Ralph Kramden in "And away we go!" pose was installed at the Miami Beach Bus Terminal.  
*   Gleason was nominated three times for an Emmy Award, but never won. (Carney and Kean did, however.)  
*   In 1976 at the Sixth Annual American Guild of Variety Artists (AGVA) "Entertainer of the Year Awards", Paul Lynde received an award for being voted the funniest man of the year.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-76) Lynde immediately turned his award over to host Jackie Gleason, citing him as "the funniest man ever." The unexpected gesture shocked Gleason.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-77)  

### Later years, health problems and death
*   On June 30, 1988, the Sunset ParkMTA, NYCT's 5th Avenue Bus Depot in Brooklyn was renamed the Jackie Gleason Depot in honor of the native Brooklynite.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-78)  
*   A statue of Gleason as Ralph Kramden in his bus driver's uniform was dedicated in August 2000 in New York City in Manhattan at the 40th Street entrance of the Port Authority Bus Terminal (PABT). The statue was briefly shown in the film _World Trade Center_ (2006).  
*   A city park in Lauderhill, Florida, was named the "Jackie Gleason Park" in his honor; it is located near his former home and features racquetball and basketball courts and a children's playground.  
*   Signs on the Brooklyn Bridge which advise drivers that they are entering Brooklyn have the Gleason phrase "How Sweet It Is!"  
*   Late in his life actor-playwright Jason Miller, Gleason's former son-in-law, was writing a screenplay based on Gleason's life. He died before it was completed.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-Linda-52)  
*   Gleason was portrayed by Brad Garrett in a 2002 television biopic about his life.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Gleason#cite_note-80)

# The History
Of Babcock Ranch

# The History
## AN INNOVATIVE HISTORY
Inspired by a bold vision and deep respect for the land, Babcock Ranch’s creation was led by Syd Kitson, Chairman and CEO of Kitson & Partners, to become America’s first solar-powered town.
Honoring the heritage of Southwest Florida while embracing innovation, its founding enabled the largest preservation land purchase in Florida’s history and the creation of the 73,000-acre Babcock Ranch Preserve.

# The History
## AN INSPIRED VISION
Today, half of the town’s 18,000 acres are dedicated to greenways, parks, and lakes. From water-conserving landscapes to energy-efficient homes and solar fields that produce more clean power than the town consumes, every element reflects a pioneering model of sustainable living — one that respects the past while building a resilient future.

In 1961, Gehry moved to Paris, where he worked for architect Andre Remonde.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-27) In 1962, he established a practice in Los Angeles that became Frank Gehry and Associates in 1967,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Templer-11) then Gehry Partners in 2001.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-28) His earliest commissions were in Southern California, where he designed a number of innovative commercial structures such as Santa Monica Place (1980) and residential buildings such as the eccentric Norton House (1984) in Venice, Los Angeles.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-29)
Among these works, Gehry's most notable design may be the renovation of his own Santa Monica residence.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-30) Originally built in 1920 and purchased by Gehry in 1977, it features a metallic exterior wrapped around the original building that leaves many of the original details visible.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-31)
Other of Gehry's buildings completed during the 1980s include the Cabrillo Marine Aquarium (1981) in San Pedro, and the California Aerospace Museum (1984) at the California Museum of Science and Industry in Los Angeles.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-k700-32)
In 1989, Gehry received the Pritzker Architecture Prize, where the jury described him: "Always open to experimentation, he has as well a sureness and maturity that resists, in the same way that Picasso did, being bound either by critical acceptance or his successes. His buildings are juxtaposed collages of spaces and materials that make users appreciative of both the theatre and the back-stage, simultaneously revealed."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-33)

Gehry continued to design other notable buildings in California, such as the Chiat/Day Building (1991) in Venice, in collaboration with Claes Oldenburg, which is well known for its massive sculpture of binoculars.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-34) He also began receiving larger national and international commissions, including his first European commission, the Vitra International Furniture Manufacturing Facility and Design Museum in Germany, completed in 1989. It was soon followed by other major commissions including the Frederick Weisman Museum of Art[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-35) (1993) in Minneapolis, Minnesota; the Cinémathèque Française[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-36) (1994) in Paris, originally the American Center in Paris;[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-37) and the Dancing House in Prague (1996).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-38)
From 1994 to 1996 several buildings by Gehry for a public housing project were realized in Goldstein, part of Frankfurt-Schwanheim (1994). In 1997, Gehry vaulted to a new level of international acclaim[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-VF_Tyrnauer_2010-1) when the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao opened in Bilbao, Spain. Hailed by _The New Yorker_ as a "masterpiece of the 20th century", and by legendary architect Philip Johnson as "the greatest building of our time",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-VF_Tyrnauer_2010-1) the museum became famous for its striking yet aesthetically pleasing design and its positive economic effect on the city.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Moore-39)

From then on, Gehry regularly won major commissions and established himself as one of the world's most notable architects. His best-received works include several concert halls for classical music. The boisterous, curvaceous Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003) in downtown Los Angeles is the centerpiece of the neighborhood's revitalization; the _Los Angeles Times_ called it "the most effective answer to doubters, naysayers, and grumbling critics an American architect has ever produced".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-40) Gehry also designed the open-air Jay Pritzker Pavilion (2004) in Chicago's Millennium Park;[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-41) and the understated New World Center (2011) in Miami Beach, which the _LA Times_ called "a piece of architecture that dares you to underestimate it or write it off at first glance".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-lat-arch-42)
His other notable works include academic buildings such as the Stata Center (2004)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-43) at MIT, and the Peter B. LewisLibrary (2008) at Princeton University;[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-44) museums such as the Museum of Pop Culture (2000) in Seattle, Washington;[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-45) commercial buildings such as the IAC Building (2007) in New York City;[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-46) and residential buildings, such as Gehry's first skyscraper, the Beekman Tower at 8 Spruce Street (now known as 8 Spruce) in New York City (2011).[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-47)

Gehry's major international works include the Dr Chau Chak Wing Building at the University of Technology Sydney, which was completed in late 2014[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-48) and officially opened in February 2015. The A$180 million building, with its façade of more than 320,000 hand-placed bricks and glass slabs in "sweeping lines", was described as "10 out of 10" on a scale of difficulty.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Gilmore-49) Gehry said he would not design a building like the "crumpled paper bag" again.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-crumpled-50) Other of his projects include the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi on Saadiyat Island in the United Arab Emirates and the Forma skyscraper project in his hometown of Toronto.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-51) Other significant projects undertaken by Gehry such as a multi-decade renovation of the Philadelphia Museum of Art were in the design stage. In October 2013, Gehry was appointed joint architect with Foster + Partners to design the High Street phase of the development of Battersea Power Station in London, Gehry's first project there.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-52)

Some of Gehry's more prominent designs failed to go forward. In addition to unrealized designs for the Corcoran Art Gallery expansion in Washington, DC, and a new Guggenheim museum near the South Street Seaport in New York City, Gehry was notoriously dropped by developer Bruce Ratner from the Pacific Park redevelopment project in the New York City borough of Brooklyn, and in 2014 as the designer of the World Trade Center Performing Arts Center in New York City.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-53) Some stalled projects showed progress: After many years and a dismissal, Gehry was reinstated as architect for the Grand Avenue Project in Los Angeles, and though his controversial[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-56) design of the National Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial in Washington, DC had numerous delays during the approval process with the United States Congress, it was finally approved in 2014 with a modified design.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-cfaapproval-58)

In 2014, two significant, long-awaited museums designed by Gehry opened: the Biomuseo,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-59) a biodiversity museum in Panama City, Panama; and the Fondation Louis Vuitton,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-62) a modern art museum in the Bois de Boulogne park in Paris, France. Both opened to generally positive reviews.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-65)
Also in 2014, Gehry was commissioned by River LA (formerly the Los Angeles River Revitalization Corporation), a nonprofit group founded by the city of Los Angeles in 2009 to coordinate river policy, to devise a wide-ranging new plan for the river.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Hawthorne-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-67)

Gehry told the French newspaper _La Croix_ in November 2016 that French president François Hollande had assured him he could relocate to France if Donald Trump was elected President of the United States.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Perlson-69) In December, Gehry said that he had no plans to move.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-70) According to former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien, Gehry considered moving back to Canada after Trump was elected to a subsequent term in 2024.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Chretien-15)
Trump and Gehry had exchanged words in 2010 when Gehry's 8 Spruce Street, originally known as Beekman Tower, was built 1 foot (0.30 m) taller than the nearby Trump Building, which until then was New York City's tallest residential building.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Perlson-69)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-71)

Notable Gehry-designed buildings completed in the 2020s include the Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial in [Washington, DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."),[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-72) and the LUMA Arles museum in France.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-73) In 2021, noting Gehry's progress on an increasing number of significant projects in his hometown, including the Grand Avenue Project, a concert hall for the Youth Orchestra Los Angeles, and an office building for [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros."), _[The Architect's Newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Architect's\_Newspaper "The Architect's Newspaper")_ stated that "Seventy-four years after he moved there from his native Toronto, L.A. is looking more and more like Gehry Country."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-74)

## Architectural style
[edit]
Said to "defy categorisation", Gehry's work reflects a spirit of experimentation coupled with a respect for the demands of professional practice, and remained largely unaligned with broader stylistic tendencies or movements.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Power-2015-75) With his earliest educational influences rooted in modernism, Gehry's work sought to escape modernist stylistic tropes while remaining interested in some of its underlying transformative agendas. Continually working between given circumstances and unanticipated materializations, he was assessed as someone who "made us produce buildings that are fun, sculpturally exciting, good experiences", although his approach might become "less relevant as pressure mounts to do more with less".[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Power-2015-75)
Gehry's style at times seemed unfinished or even crude, but his work was consistent with the California "funk" art movement of the 1960s and early 1970s, which featured the use of inexpensive found objects and nontraditional media such as clay to make serious art.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-achille.paris-76) His works always had at least some element of deconstructivism;[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-WorldBuild365-77) he was called "the apostle of chain-link fencing and corrugated metal siding".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-78) However, a retrospective exhibit at New York's Whitney Museum in 1988 revealed that he was also a sophisticated classical artist who knew European art history and contemporary sculpture and painting.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-achille.paris-76)

## Architectural style
Gehry described architecture as inherently sculptural, asserting, "I always thought that architecture was, by definition, a three-dimensional object, therefore sculpture."[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-79) This perspective reflected his commitment to blending artistic and architectural disciplines. Gehry's early work with sculptors influenced his experimental approach, which includes deconstructing traditional architectural forms and embracing ideas of flow and defamiliarization, akin to Viktor Shklovsky's concept of "laying bare the device".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-80)
Gehry's Jewish heritage and immigrant background shaped his architectural philosophy. He often reinterpreted traditional forms in ways that reflect his multicultural experience. His works were described as embodying "a critique of consumerism" by defying expectations of luxury and focusing on creativity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-auto3-81)

## Academia and design career
[edit]
In January 2011, Gehry joined the University of Southern California (USC) faculty, as the Judge Widney Professor of Architecture.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-82) He continued in this role at his alma mater. He also held teaching positions at Harvard University, the University of California at Los Angeles, the University of Toronto, Columbia University, the Federal Institute of Technology in Zürich, and at Yale University.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-83)
Though he was often referred to as a "starchitect", he repeatedly expressed his disdain for the term, insisting he was only an architect.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Archdaily-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-85)
In February 2017, MasterClass announced an online architecture course taught by Gehry that was released July of that year.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-86)

## Academia and design career
Gehry was involved in exhibition designs at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art dating back to the 1960s. In 1965, Gehry designed the exhibition display for the "Art Treasures of Japan" exhibition at the LACMA. This was followed soon after by the exhibition design for the "Assyrian Reliefs" show in 1966 and the "Billy Al Bengston Retrospective" in 1968. The LACMA then had Gehry design the installation for the "Treasures of Tutankhamen" exhibition in 1978 followed by the "Avant-Garde in Russia 1910–1930" exhibition in 1980. The subsequent year, Gehry designed the exhibition for "Seventeen Artists in the '60s" at the LACMA, followed soon after by the "German Expressionist Sculpture Exhibition" in 1983. In 1991–92, Gehry designed the installation of the landmark exhibition "Degenerate Art: The Fate of the Avant-Garde in Nazi Germany", which opened at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and traveled to the Art Institute of Chicago, the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, and the Altes Museum in Berlin.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-88) Gehry was asked to design an exhibition on the work of Alexander Calder at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art's Resnick Pavilion, again invited by the museum's curator Stephanie Barron.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-89)
In addition to his long-standing involvement with exhibition design at the LACMA, Gehry also designed numerous exhibition installations with other institutions. In 1998, "The Art of the Motorcycle" exhibition opened at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum with its installation designed by Gehry.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-90)

## Academia and design career
As a result of his fascination, the first Fish Lamps were fabricated between 1984 and 1986. They employed wire armatures molded into fish shapes, onto which shards of plastic laminate ColorCore are individually glued. Since the creation of the first lamp in 1984, the fish has become a recurrent motif in Gehry's work, most notably in the _Fish Sculpture_ at La Vila Olímpica del Poblenou in Barcelona (1989–92) and _Standing Glass Fish_ for the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden (1986).[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-101)
Gehry-designed kettle, presented in the Indianapolis Museum of Art
Gehry collaborated with luxury jewelry company Tiffany & Co., creating six distinct jewelry collections: the Orchid, Fish, Torque, Equus, Axis, and Fold collections. In addition to jewelry, Gehry designed other items, including a distinctive collector's chess set and a series of tableware items, including vases, cups, and bowls for the company.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-gizmodo-102)
In 2004, Gehry designed the official trophy for the World Cup of Hockey.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-103) He redesigned the trophy for the next tournament in 2016.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-104)
He collaborated with American furniture manufacturer Emeco on designs such as the 2004 "Superlight" chair.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-106)
In 2014, Gehry was one of the six "iconoclasts" selected by French fashion house Louis Vuitton to design a piece using their iconic monogram pattern as part of their "Celebrating Monogram" campaign.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-monogram-107)

## Academia and design career
In 2015, Gehry designed his first yacht.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-108)
In 2020, Gehry designed a limited edition bottle of Hennessy cognac.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-109)

## Academia and design career
### Software development
[edit]
Gehry's firm was responsible for innovation in architectural software.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYT2009-110) His firm spun off another firm called Gehry Technologies that was established in 2002. In 2005, Gehry Technologies began a partnership with Dassault Systèmes to bring innovations from the aerospace and manufacturing world to AEC and developed Digital Project software, as well as GTeam software. The 3D modelling and project management features of this software were effective in implementing Gehry's novel and complex designs under budget. For example, the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao was completed for $3M less than its budget of $100M.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYT2009-110) In 2014, Gehry Technologies was acquired by software company Trimble Navigation.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-o540-112)

## Personal life and death
[edit]
Gehry became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 1951, several years after he and his family moved to Los Angeles.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-LATobit-113)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-114) He lost his Canadian citizenship as dual citizenship was not an option at the time. Prime Minister Jean Chrétien restored Gehry's Canadian citizenship in 2002.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Chretien-15) He lived in Santa Monica, California, and practiced out of Los Angeles.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-115) Having grown up in Canada, he was an avid fan of ice hockey. He began a hockey league, FOG (for Frank Owen Gehry), in his office, and continued to play the game until around the age of 80.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-goldberger-116)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Verge-14) In 2004, he designed the trophy for the World Cup of Hockey.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-117)
In 1952, Gehry married Anita Snyder; in 1966, they were divorced.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-guardian-bio-2) In 1975, he married Berta Aguilera.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-guardian-bio-2)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYTobit-118)

## Personal life and death
Gehry was known for his occasional bad temper. During a trip to Oviedo to accept the Prince of Asturias Award in October 2014, he received a significant amount of attention, both positive and negative, for publicly flipping off a reporter at a press conference who accused him of being a "showy" architect.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-120)
He was a member of the California Yacht Club in Marina Del Rey, and enjoyed sailing with his fiberglass-hulled yacht, _Foggy_.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-nytimes-121)
On December 5, 2025, Gehry died at the age of 96 from a respiratory condition at his home in Santa Monica.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYTobit-118)
In 2014, Gehry co-founded Turnaround Arts: California, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that expands access to the arts in under-resourced public elementary and middle schools across California.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-122)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-123) In addition to serving as a board member for the organization, Gehry served as a visiting artist with students.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-124) He also served on the leadership council of the New York Stem Cell Foundation.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-nyscf-125)

texts.7:
Gehry continued to design other notable buildings in California, such as the Chiat/Day Building (1991) in Venice, in collaboration with Claes Oldenburg, which is well known for its massive sculpture of binoculars.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-34) He also began receiving larger national and international commissions, including his first European commission, the Vitra International Furniture Manufacturing Facility and Design Museum in Germany, completed in 1989. It was soon followed by other major commissions including the Frederick Weisman Museum of Art[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-35) (1993) in Minneapolis, Minnesota; the Cinémathèque Française[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-36) (1994) in Paris, originally the American Center in Paris;[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-37) and the Dancing House in Prague (1996).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-38)
From 1994 to 1996 several buildings by Gehry for a public housing project were realized in Goldstein, part of Frankfurt-Schwanheim (1994). In 1997, Gehry vaulted to a new level of international acclaim[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-VF_Tyrnauer_2010-1) when the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao opened in Bilbao, Spain. Hailed by _The New Yorker_ as a "masterpiece of the 20th century", and by legendary architect Philip Johnson as "the greatest building of our time",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-VF_Tyrnauer_2010-1) the museum became famous for its striking yet aesthetically pleasing design and its positive economic effect on the city.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Moore-39)
texts.8:
From then on, Gehry regularly won major commissions and established himself as one of the world's most notable architects. His best-received works include several concert halls for classical music. The boisterous, curvaceous Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003) in downtown Los Angeles is the centerpiece of the neighborhood's revitalization; the _Los Angeles Times_ called it "the most effective answer to doubters, naysayers, and grumbling critics an American architect has ever produced".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-40) Gehry also designed the open-air Jay Pritzker Pavilion (2004) in Chicago's Millennium Park;[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-41) and the understated New World Center (2011) in Miami Beach, which the _LA Times_ called "a piece of architecture that dares you to underestimate it or write it off at first glance".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-lat-arch-42)
His other notable works include academic buildings such as the Stata Center (2004)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-43) at MIT, and the Peter B. LewisLibrary (2008) at Princeton University;[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-44) museums such as the Museum of Pop Culture (2000) in Seattle, Washington;[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-45) commercial buildings such as the IAC Building (2007) in New York City;[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-46) and residential buildings, such as Gehry's first skyscraper, the Beekman Tower at 8 Spruce Street (now known as 8 Spruce) in New York City (2011).[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-47)
texts.9: Gehry's major international works include the Dr Chau Chak Wing Building at the University of Technology Sydney, which was completed in late 2014[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-48) and officially opened in February 2015. The A$180 million building, with its façade of more than 320,000 hand-placed bricks and glass slabs in "sweeping lines", was described as "10 out of 10" on a scale of difficulty.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Gilmore-49) Gehry said he would not design a building like the "crumpled paper bag" again.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-crumpled-50) Other of his projects include the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi on Saadiyat Island in the United Arab Emirates and the Forma skyscraper project in his hometown of Toronto.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-51) Other significant projects undertaken by Gehry such as a multi-decade renovation of the Philadelphia Museum of Art were in the design stage. In October 2013, Gehry was appointed joint architect with Foster + Partners to design the High Street phase of the development of Battersea Power Station in London, Gehry's first project there.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-52)
texts.10: Some of Gehry's more prominent designs failed to go forward. In addition to unrealized designs for the Corcoran Art Gallery expansion in Washington, DC, and a new Guggenheim museum near the South Street Seaport in New York City, Gehry was notoriously dropped by developer Bruce Ratner from the Pacific Park redevelopment project in the New York City borough of Brooklyn, and in 2014 as the designer of the World Trade Center Performing Arts Center in New York City.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-53) Some stalled projects showed progress: After many years and a dismissal, Gehry was reinstated as architect for the Grand Avenue Project in Los Angeles, and though his controversial[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-56) design of the National Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial in Washington, DC had numerous delays during the approval process with the United States Congress, it was finally approved in 2014 with a modified design.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-cfaapproval-58)
texts.11:
In 2014, two significant, long-awaited museums designed by Gehry opened: the Biomuseo,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-59) a biodiversity museum in Panama City, Panama; and the Fondation Louis Vuitton,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-62) a modern art museum in the Bois de Boulogne park in Paris, France. Both opened to generally positive reviews.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-65)
Also in 2014, Gehry was commissioned by River LA (formerly the Los Angeles River Revitalization Corporation), a nonprofit group founded by the city of Los Angeles in 2009 to coordinate river policy, to devise a wide-ranging new plan for the river.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Hawthorne-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-67)
texts.12:
Gehry told the French newspaper _La Croix_ in November 2016 that French president François Hollande had assured him he could relocate to France if Donald Trump was elected President of the United States.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Perlson-69) In December, Gehry said that he had no plans to move.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-70) According to former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien, Gehry considered moving back to Canada after Trump was elected to a subsequent term in 2024.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Chretien-15)
Trump and Gehry had exchanged words in 2010 when Gehry's 8 Spruce Street, originally known as Beekman Tower, was built 1 foot (0.30 m) taller than the nearby Trump Building, which until then was New York City's tallest residential building.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Perlson-69)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-71)
texts.13: Notable Gehry-designed buildings completed in the 2020s include the Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial in [Washington, DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."),[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-72) and the LUMA Arles museum in France.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-73) In 2021, noting Gehry's progress on an increasing number of significant projects in his hometown, including the Grand Avenue Project, a concert hall for the Youth Orchestra Los Angeles, and an office building for [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros."), _[The Architect's Newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Architect's\_Newspaper "The Architect's Newspaper")_ stated that "Seventy-four years after he moved there from his native Toronto, L.A. is looking more and more like Gehry Country."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-74)
texts.14:
## Architectural style
[edit]
Said to "defy categorisation", Gehry's work reflects a spirit of experimentation coupled with a respect for the demands of professional practice, and remained largely unaligned with broader stylistic tendencies or movements.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Power-2015-75) With his earliest educational influences rooted in modernism, Gehry's work sought to escape modernist stylistic tropes while remaining interested in some of its underlying transformative agendas. Continually working between given circumstances and unanticipated materializations, he was assessed as someone who "made us produce buildings that are fun, sculpturally exciting, good experiences", although his approach might become "less relevant as pressure mounts to do more with less".[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Power-2015-75)
Gehry's style at times seemed unfinished or even crude, but his work was consistent with the California "funk" art movement of the 1960s and early 1970s, which featured the use of inexpensive found objects and nontraditional media such as clay to make serious art.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-achille.paris-76) His works always had at least some element of deconstructivism;[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-WorldBuild365-77) he was called "the apostle of chain-link fencing and corrugated metal siding".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-78) However, a retrospective exhibit at New York's Whitney Museum in 1988 revealed that he was also a sophisticated classical artist who knew European art history and contemporary sculpture and painting.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-achille.paris-76)
texts.15:
## Architectural style
Gehry described architecture as inherently sculptural, asserting, "I always thought that architecture was, by definition, a three-dimensional object, therefore sculpture."[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-79) This perspective reflected his commitment to blending artistic and architectural disciplines. Gehry's early work with sculptors influenced his experimental approach, which includes deconstructing traditional architectural forms and embracing ideas of flow and defamiliarization, akin to Viktor Shklovsky's concept of "laying bare the device".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-80)
Gehry's Jewish heritage and immigrant background shaped his architectural philosophy. He often reinterpreted traditional forms in ways that reflect his multicultural experience. His works were described as embodying "a critique of consumerism" by defying expectations of luxury and focusing on creativity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-auto3-81)

texts.16:
## Academia and design career
[edit]
In January 2011, Gehry joined the University of Southern California (USC) faculty, as the Judge Widney Professor of Architecture.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-82) He continued in this role at his alma mater. He also held teaching positions at Harvard University, the University of California at Los Angeles, the University of Toronto, Columbia University, the Federal Institute of Technology in Zürich, and at Yale University.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-83)
Though he was often referred to as a "starchitect", he repeatedly expressed his disdain for the term, insisting he was only an architect.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Archdaily-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-85)
In February 2017, MasterClass announced an online architecture course taught by Gehry that was released July of that year.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-86)
texts.17:
## Academia and design career
Gehry was involved in exhibition designs at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art dating back to the 1960s. In 1965, Gehry designed the exhibition display for the "Art Treasures of Japan" exhibition at the LACMA. This was followed soon after by the exhibition design for the "Assyrian Reliefs" show in 1966 and the "Billy Al Bengston Retrospective" in 1968. The LACMA then had Gehry design the installation for the "Treasures of Tutankhamen" exhibition in 1978 followed by the "Avant-Garde in Russia 1910–1930" exhibition in 1980. The subsequent year, Gehry designed the exhibition for "Seventeen Artists in the '60s" at the LACMA, followed soon after by the "German Expressionist Sculpture Exhibition" in 1983. In 1991–92, Gehry designed the installation of the landmark exhibition "Degenerate Art: The Fate of the Avant-Garde in Nazi Germany", which opened at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and traveled to the Art Institute of Chicago, the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, and the Altes Museum in Berlin.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-88) Gehry was asked to design an exhibition on the work of Alexander Calder at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art's Resnick Pavilion, again invited by the museum's curator Stephanie Barron.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-89)
In addition to his long-standing involvement with exhibition design at the LACMA, Gehry also designed numerous exhibition installations with other institutions. In 1998, "The Art of the Motorcycle" exhibition opened at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum with its installation designed by Gehry.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-90)
texts.20:
## Academia and design career
As a result of his fascination, the first Fish Lamps were fabricated between 1984 and 1986. They employed wire armatures molded into fish shapes, onto which shards of plastic laminate ColorCore are individually glued. Since the creation of the first lamp in 1984, the fish has become a recurrent motif in Gehry's work, most notably in the _Fish Sculpture_ at La Vila Olímpica del Poblenou in Barcelona (1989–92) and _Standing Glass Fish_ for the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden (1986).[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-101)
Gehry-designed kettle, presented in the Indianapolis Museum of Art
Gehry collaborated with luxury jewelry company Tiffany & Co., creating six distinct jewelry collections: the Orchid, Fish, Torque, Equus, Axis, and Fold collections. In addition to jewelry, Gehry designed other items, including a distinctive collector's chess set and a series of tableware items, including vases, cups, and bowls for the company.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-gizmodo-102)
In 2004, Gehry designed the official trophy for the World Cup of Hockey.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-103) He redesigned the trophy for the next tournament in 2016.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-104)
He collaborated with American furniture manufacturer Emeco on designs such as the 2004 "Superlight" chair.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-106)
In 2014, Gehry was one of the six "iconoclasts" selected by French fashion house Louis Vuitton to design a piece using their iconic monogram pattern as part of their "Celebrating Monogram" campaign.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-monogram-107)
texts.21:
## Academia and design career
In 2015, Gehry designed his first yacht.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-108)
In 2020, Gehry designed a limited edition bottle of Hennessy cognac.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-109)
texts.22:
## Academia and design career
### Software development
[edit]
Gehry's firm was responsible for innovation in architectural software.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYT2009-110) His firm spun off another firm called Gehry Technologies that was established in 2002. In 2005, Gehry Technologies began a partnership with Dassault Systèmes to bring innovations from the aerospace and manufacturing world to AEC and developed Digital Project software, as well as GTeam software. The 3D modelling and project management features of this software were effective in implementing Gehry's novel and complex designs under budget. For example, the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao was completed for $3M less than its budget of $100M.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYT2009-110) In 2014, Gehry Technologies was acquired by software company Trimble Navigation.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-o540-112)
texts.23:
## Personal life and death
[edit]
Gehry became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 1951, several years after he and his family moved to Los Angeles.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-LATobit-113)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-114) He lost his Canadian citizenship as dual citizenship was not an option at the time. Prime Minister Jean Chrétien restored Gehry's Canadian citizenship in 2002.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Chretien-15) He lived in Santa Monica, California, and practiced out of Los Angeles.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-115) Having grown up in Canada, he was an avid fan of ice hockey. He began a hockey league, FOG (for Frank Owen Gehry), in his office, and continued to play the game until around the age of 80.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-goldberger-116)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Verge-14) In 2004, he designed the trophy for the World Cup of Hockey.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-117)
In 1952, Gehry married Anita Snyder; in 1966, they were divorced.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-guardian-bio-2) In 1975, he married Berta Aguilera.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-guardian-bio-2)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYTobit-118)
texts.24:
## Personal life and death
Gehry was known for his occasional bad temper. During a trip to Oviedo to accept the Prince of Asturias Award in October 2014, he received a significant amount of attention, both positive and negative, for publicly flipping off a reporter at a press conference who accused him of being a "showy" architect.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-120)
He was a member of the California Yacht Club in Marina Del Rey, and enjoyed sailing with his fiberglass-hulled yacht, _Foggy_.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-nytimes-121)
On December 5, 2025, Gehry died at the age of 96 from a respiratory condition at his home in Santa Monica.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYTobit-118)
In 2014, Gehry co-founded Turnaround Arts: California, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that expands access to the arts in under-resourced public elementary and middle schools across California.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-122)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-123) In addition to serving as a board member for the organization, Gehry served as a visiting artist with students.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-124) He also served on the leadership council of the New York Stem Cell Foundation.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-nyscf-125)

Hailed by _The New Yorker_ as a "masterpiece of the 20th century", and by legendary architect Philip Johnson as "the greatest building of our time",[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-VF_Tyrnauer_2010-1) the museum became famous for its striking yet aesthetically pleasing design and its positive economic effect on the city.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Moore-39)

From then on, Gehry regularly won major commissions and established himself as one of the world's most notable architects. His best-received works include several concert halls for classical music. The boisterous, curvaceous Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003) in downtown Los Angeles is the centerpiece of the neighborhood's revitalization; the _Los Angeles Times_ called it "the most effective answer to doubters, naysayers, and grumbling critics an American architect has ever produced".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-40) Gehry also designed the open-air Jay Pritzker Pavilion (2004) in Chicago's Millennium Park;[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-41) and the understated New World Center (2011) in Miami Beach, which the _LA Times_ called "a piece of architecture that dares you to underestimate it or write it off at first glance".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-lat-arch-42)
His other notable works include academic buildings such as the Stata Center (2004)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-43) at MIT, and the Peter B. LewisLibrary (2008) at Princeton University;[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-44) museums such as the Museum of Pop Culture (2000) in Seattle, Washington;[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-45) commercial buildings such as the IAC Building (2007) in New York City;[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-46) and residential buildings, such as Gehry's first skyscraper, the Beekman Tower at 8 Spruce Street (now known as 8 Spruce) in New York City (2011).[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-47)

Gehry's major international works include the Dr Chau Chak Wing Building at the University of Technology Sydney, which was completed in late 2014[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-48) and officially opened in February 2015. The A$180 million building, with its façade of more than 320,000 hand-placed bricks and glass slabs in "sweeping lines", was described as "10 out of 10" on a scale of difficulty.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Gilmore-49) Gehry said he would not design a building like the "crumpled paper bag" again.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-crumpled-50) Other of his projects include the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi on Saadiyat Island in the United Arab Emirates and the Forma skyscraper project in his hometown of Toronto.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-51) Other significant projects undertaken by Gehry such as a multi-decade renovation of the Philadelphia Museum of Art were in the design stage. In October 2013, Gehry was appointed joint architect with Foster + Partners to design the High Street phase of the development of Battersea Power Station in London, Gehry's first project there.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-52)

Some of Gehry's more prominent designs failed to go forward. In addition to unrealized designs for the Corcoran Art Gallery expansion in Washington, DC, and a new Guggenheim museum near the South Street Seaport in New York City, Gehry was notoriously dropped by developer Bruce Ratner from the Pacific Park redevelopment project in the New York City borough of Brooklyn, and in 2014 as the designer of the World Trade Center Performing Arts Center in New York City.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-53) Some stalled projects showed progress: After many years and a dismissal, Gehry was reinstated as architect for the Grand Avenue Project in Los Angeles, and though his controversial[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-56) design of the National Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial in Washington, DC had numerous delays during the approval process with the United States Congress, it was finally approved in 2014 with a modified design.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-cfaapproval-58)

In 2014, two significant, long-awaited museums designed by Gehry opened: the Biomuseo,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-59) a biodiversity museum in Panama City, Panama; and the Fondation Louis Vuitton,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-62) a modern art museum in the Bois de Boulogne park in Paris, France. Both opened to generally positive reviews.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-65)
Also in 2014, Gehry was commissioned by River LA (formerly the Los Angeles River Revitalization Corporation), a nonprofit group founded by the city of Los Angeles in 2009 to coordinate river policy, to devise a wide-ranging new plan for the river.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Hawthorne-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-67)

Gehry told the French newspaper _La Croix_ in November 2016 that French president François Hollande had assured him he could relocate to France if Donald Trump was elected President of the United States.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Perlson-69) In December, Gehry said that he had no plans to move.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-70) According to former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien, Gehry considered moving back to Canada after Trump was elected to a subsequent term in 2024.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Chretien-15)
Trump and Gehry had exchanged words in 2010 when Gehry's 8 Spruce Street, originally known as Beekman Tower, was built 1 foot (0.30 m) taller than the nearby Trump Building, which until then was New York City's tallest residential building.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Perlson-69)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-71)

Notable Gehry-designed buildings completed in the 2020s include the Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial in [Washington, DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."),[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-72) and the LUMA Arles museum in France.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-73) In 2021, noting Gehry's progress on an increasing number of significant projects in his hometown, including the Grand Avenue Project, a concert hall for the Youth Orchestra Los Angeles, and an office building for [Warner Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros. "Warner Bros."), _[The Architect's Newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Architect's\_Newspaper "The Architect's Newspaper")_ stated that "Seventy-four years after he moved there from his native Toronto, L.A. is looking more and more like Gehry Country."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-74)

## Architectural style
[edit]
Said to "defy categorisation", Gehry's work reflects a spirit of experimentation coupled with a respect for the demands of professional practice, and remained largely unaligned with broader stylistic tendencies or movements.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Power-2015-75) With his earliest educational influences rooted in modernism, Gehry's work sought to escape modernist stylistic tropes while remaining interested in some of its underlying transformative agendas. Continually working between given circumstances and unanticipated materializations, he was assessed as someone who "made us produce buildings that are fun, sculpturally exciting, good experiences", although his approach might become "less relevant as pressure mounts to do more with less".[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Power-2015-75)
Gehry's style at times seemed unfinished or even crude, but his work was consistent with the California "funk" art movement of the 1960s and early 1970s, which featured the use of inexpensive found objects and nontraditional media such as clay to make serious art.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-achille.paris-76) His works always had at least some element of deconstructivism;[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-WorldBuild365-77) he was called "the apostle of chain-link fencing and corrugated metal siding".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-78) However, a retrospective exhibit at New York's Whitney Museum in 1988 revealed that he was also a sophisticated classical artist who knew European art history and contemporary sculpture and painting.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-achille.paris-76)

## Architectural style
Gehry described architecture as inherently sculptural, asserting, "I always thought that architecture was, by definition, a three-dimensional object, therefore sculpture."[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-79) This perspective reflected his commitment to blending artistic and architectural disciplines. Gehry's early work with sculptors influenced his experimental approach, which includes deconstructing traditional architectural forms and embracing ideas of flow and defamiliarization, akin to Viktor Shklovsky's concept of "laying bare the device".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-80)
Gehry's Jewish heritage and immigrant background shaped his architectural philosophy. He often reinterpreted traditional forms in ways that reflect his multicultural experience. His works were described as embodying "a critique of consumerism" by defying expectations of luxury and focusing on creativity.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-auto3-81)

## Academia and design career
[edit]
In January 2011, Gehry joined the University of Southern California (USC) faculty, as the Judge Widney Professor of Architecture.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-82) He continued in this role at his alma mater. He also held teaching positions at Harvard University, the University of California at Los Angeles, the University of Toronto, Columbia University, the Federal Institute of Technology in Zürich, and at Yale University.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-83)
Though he was often referred to as a "starchitect", he repeatedly expressed his disdain for the term, insisting he was only an architect.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Archdaily-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-85)
In February 2017, MasterClass announced an online architecture course taught by Gehry that was released July of that year.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-86)

## Academia and design career
Gehry was involved in exhibition designs at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art dating back to the 1960s. In 1965, Gehry designed the exhibition display for the "Art Treasures of Japan" exhibition at the LACMA. This was followed soon after by the exhibition design for the "Assyrian Reliefs" show in 1966 and the "Billy Al Bengston Retrospective" in 1968. The LACMA then had Gehry design the installation for the "Treasures of Tutankhamen" exhibition in 1978 followed by the "Avant-Garde in Russia 1910–1930" exhibition in 1980. The subsequent year, Gehry designed the exhibition for "Seventeen Artists in the '60s" at the LACMA, followed soon after by the "German Expressionist Sculpture Exhibition" in 1983. In 1991–92, Gehry designed the installation of the landmark exhibition "Degenerate Art: The Fate of the Avant-Garde in Nazi Germany", which opened at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and traveled to the Art Institute of Chicago, the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, and the Altes Museum in Berlin.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-88) Gehry was asked to design an exhibition on the work of Alexander Calder at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art's Resnick Pavilion, again invited by the museum's curator Stephanie Barron.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-89)
In addition to his long-standing involvement with exhibition design at the LACMA, Gehry also designed numerous exhibition installations with other institutions. In 1998, "The Art of the Motorcycle" exhibition opened at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum with its installation designed by Gehry.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-90)

## Academia and design career
As a result of his fascination, the first Fish Lamps were fabricated between 1984 and 1986. They employed wire armatures molded into fish shapes, onto which shards of plastic laminate ColorCore are individually glued. Since the creation of the first lamp in 1984, the fish has become a recurrent motif in Gehry's work, most notably in the _Fish Sculpture_ at La Vila Olímpica del Poblenou in Barcelona (1989–92) and _Standing Glass Fish_ for the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden (1986).[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-101)
Gehry-designed kettle, presented in the Indianapolis Museum of Art
Gehry collaborated with luxury jewelry company Tiffany & Co., creating six distinct jewelry collections: the Orchid, Fish, Torque, Equus, Axis, and Fold collections. In addition to jewelry, Gehry designed other items, including a distinctive collector's chess set and a series of tableware items, including vases, cups, and bowls for the company.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-gizmodo-102)
In 2004, Gehry designed the official trophy for the World Cup of Hockey.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-103) He redesigned the trophy for the next tournament in 2016.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-104)
He collaborated with American furniture manufacturer Emeco on designs such as the 2004 "Superlight" chair.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-106)
In 2014, Gehry was one of the six "iconoclasts" selected by French fashion house Louis Vuitton to design a piece using their iconic monogram pattern as part of their "Celebrating Monogram" campaign.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-monogram-107)

## Academia and design career
In 2015, Gehry designed his first yacht.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-108)
In 2020, Gehry designed a limited edition bottle of Hennessy cognac.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-109)

## Academia and design career
### Software development
[edit]
Gehry's firm was responsible for innovation in architectural software.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYT2009-110) His firm spun off another firm called Gehry Technologies that was established in 2002. In 2005, Gehry Technologies began a partnership with Dassault Systèmes to bring innovations from the aerospace and manufacturing world to AEC and developed Digital Project software, as well as GTeam software. The 3D modelling and project management features of this software were effective in implementing Gehry's novel and complex designs under budget. For example, the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao was completed for $3M less than its budget of $100M.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYT2009-110) In 2014, Gehry Technologies was acquired by software company Trimble Navigation.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-o540-112)

## Personal life and death
[edit]
Gehry became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 1951, several years after he and his family moved to Los Angeles.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-LATobit-113)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-114) He lost his Canadian citizenship as dual citizenship was not an option at the time. Prime Minister Jean Chrétien restored Gehry's Canadian citizenship in 2002.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Chretien-15) He lived in Santa Monica, California, and practiced out of Los Angeles.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-115) Having grown up in Canada, he was an avid fan of ice hockey. He began a hockey league, FOG (for Frank Owen Gehry), in his office, and continued to play the game until around the age of 80.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-goldberger-116)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-Verge-14) In 2004, he designed the trophy for the World Cup of Hockey.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-117)
In 1952, Gehry married Anita Snyder; in 1966, they were divorced.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-guardian-bio-2) In 1975, he married Berta Aguilera.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-guardian-bio-2)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYTobit-118)

## Personal life and death
Gehry was known for his occasional bad temper. During a trip to Oviedo to accept the Prince of Asturias Award in October 2014, he received a significant amount of attention, both positive and negative, for publicly flipping off a reporter at a press conference who accused him of being a "showy" architect.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-119)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-120)
He was a member of the California Yacht Club in Marina Del Rey, and enjoyed sailing with his fiberglass-hulled yacht, _Foggy_.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-nytimes-121)
On December 5, 2025, Gehry died at the age of 96 from a respiratory condition at his home in Santa Monica.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-NYTobit-118)
In 2014, Gehry co-founded Turnaround Arts: California, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that expands access to the arts in under-resourced public elementary and middle schools across California.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-122)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-123) In addition to serving as a board member for the organization, Gehry served as a visiting artist with students.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-124) He also served on the leadership council of the New York Stem Cell Foundation.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Gehry#cite_note-nyscf-125)
