**Jane Holzer** (née**Brukenfeld**; born October 23, 1940), also known as **Baby Jane**, is an American model, actress, art collector, and real estate investor. She rose to prominence during the 1960s as Pop artist Andy Warhol's first "Superstar."
Known for her voluminous teased blonde hair, Holzer emerged as an influential figure in the international fashion scene and became emblematic of a new form of media celebrity in the 1960s. A muse to photographer David Bailey, she was described by _Vogue_ editor-in-chief Diana Vreeland as "the most contemporary girl I know." She appeared on the cover of British _Vogue_ and _Show_ magazine in 1964. That same year, journalist Tom Wolfe heralded her as the "Girl of the Year," recognizing her as a symbol of the era's emerging youth culture and changing social landscape. Holzer starred in several of Warhol's underground films, including _Soap Opera_ (1964), _Couch_ (1964), _Batman Dracula_ (1964), and _Camp_ (1965). In 1966, _[Women's Wear Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's\_Wear\_Daily "Women's Wear Daily")_ named her one of New York's "fashion revolutionaries." She later established a successful career as a real estate investor in Palm Beach.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Jane Brukenfeld was born and raised in Palm Beach, Florida, the daughter of real estate and insurance investor Carl Brukenfeld (1906–1962).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:3-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:13-2) Her family's wealth derived from extensive real estate holdings throughout Florida, including numerous properties in Palm Beach and more than eight miles of oceanfront land on Merritt Island, now part of Cape Canaveral.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:3-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:1-3) Her father and grandfather, Morris Brukenfeld, were active in the development of Worth Avenue, helping to found the Worth Avenue Merchants Association and constructing several commercial buildings along the avenue.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:13-2) In 1951, her father established the Brukenfeld Family Foundation, a philanthropic organization.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-4)
She grew up in a Jewish household and attended Palm Beach High School for a year before transferring to Cherry Lawn School in Darien, Connecticut.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965215-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:12-6)
Brukenfeld was admitted to Finch Junior College in Manhattan, but she spent most of her time at dancing at El Morocco, and "flunked out of college on purpose to become a model."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965216-7)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:1-3)

## Early life and education
### Early modeling career
[edit]
Before her marriage, Jane Holzer modeled professionally under her maiden name, Jane Brukenfeld, in New York and Paris.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8) She was scheduled to walk in Hubert de Givenchy's Paris couture presentations but left the city shortly before the shows to marry Leonard Holzer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8)
In April 1963, the British magazine _Tatler and Bystander_ profiled Holzer in its series of beauty in fashion, describing her as an elegant young American socialite whose style was reminiscent of Grace Kelly.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8) The magazine highlighted her Paris wardrobe, her preference for the designs of Coco Chanel, Balenciaga, Yves Saint Laurent, and Hermès, and suggested that she was a future contender for the International Best Dressed List.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8) It also compared her appearance to that of Italian actress Monica Vitti.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8)
Later in 1963, Holzer's modeling career gained momentum after she traveled to London, where she was photographed by David Bailey.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965216-7) In a 1964 interview with Tom Wolfe, Holzer credited Bailey with launching her career, saying, "Bailey created four girls that summer. He created Jean Shrimpton, he created me, he created Angela Howard and Susan Murray. There's no photographer like that in America. Avedon hasn’t done that for a girl, Penn hasn't, and Bailey created four girls in one summer. He did some pictures of me for the English _Vogue_, and that was all it took."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965216-7)

## Early life and education
### Early modeling career

In 1966, Holzer launched a brief singing career with the record "Boy You're Gonna Hurt Yourself."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:8-34) She promoted the song with performances on the television programs _Hullabaloo_ and _The Lloyd Thaxton Show_ in March 1966.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-38) Holzer intended to wear a nearly transparent plastic dress on _Hullabaloo_ but was asked by the show's producer to change before filming.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-39) The publicity surrounding the appearance led to two recording contract offers.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-40) In 1967, she released the Atco Records single "Rapunzel"/"Nowhere," produced by Al Kasha and arranged by Barry Goldberg.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-41)

# Dina Merrill, Heiress Turned Actress Who Grew Up in Trump’s Future Mar-a-Lago Estate, Dies at 93
Merrill starred in ’60s classics like “BUtterfield 8” and “The Courtship of Eddie’s Father”
Thom Geier

# Dina Merrill, Heiress Turned Actress Who Grew Up in Trump’s Future Mar-a-Lago Estate, Dies at 93
## Share on Social Media

Getty Images
**Getting your Trinity Audio player ready…**
Dina Merrill, an heiress turned actress who starred in classic movies such as 1960’s “BUtterfield 8” and 1963’s “The Courtship of Eddie’s Father” died Monday in East Hampton, New York, the New York Timesreported. She was 93.
Her death was confirmed by , Stanley H. Rumbough, who said she suffered from Lewy Body dementia.
The daughter of Wall Street giant E.F. Hutton and cereal scion Marjorie Merriweather Post, Merrill grew up surrounded by wealth.
According to the Times, she spent up to half of each year as a child on the family’s giant yacht, the Sea Cloud, and the other half on a 115-room estate in Mar-a-Lago, Florida, that was renovated into a private club after its purchase by future U.S. President Donald Trump in 1985. (Ivanka Trump shared the same childhood bedroom suite, the Times wrote.)

# Dina Merrill, Heiress Turned Actress Who Grew Up in Trump’s Future Mar-a-Lago Estate, Dies at 93
## Share on Social Media
Merrill defied her father’s wishes by becoming an actress, making her Broadway debut in 1945’s “The Mermaids Singing.” But she was 34 by the time she got her first movie role — in the 1957 Katharine Hepburn-Spencer Tracy comedy “The Desk Set” — because she took time out to raise three children with her first husband, the Colgate-Palmolive heir Stanley M. Rumbough Jr. (The couple divorced in 1966.)
But then she landed a series of high-profile roles in Hollywood, as the daughter of a Wall Street banker in 1959’s “What Makes Sammy Run” and as jilted wives in “BUtterfield 8” opposite Liz Taylor and “The Courtship of Eddie’s Father” with Glenn Ford and Shirley Jones.
Other noteworthy roles included 1959’s “Operation Petticoat,” 1960’s “The Sundowners,” 1961’s “the Young Savages” and Robert Altman’s 1992 Hollywood comedy “The Player.”
In 1966, Merrill married actor Cliff Robertson — though they divorced in 1989. She then married actor turned film producer Ted Hartley.
Merrill was a moderate Republican who served as vice chair for the Republican Pro-Choice Coalition and vice president of the New York Mission Society, the Times wrote. She also contributed heavily to the Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation.

**Jane Holzer** (née**Brukenfeld**; born October 23, 1940), also known as **Baby Jane**, is an American model, actress, art collector, and real estate investor. She rose to prominence during the 1960s as Pop artist Andy Warhol's first "Superstar."
Known for her voluminous teased blonde hair, Holzer emerged as an influential figure in the international fashion scene and became emblematic of a new form of media celebrity in the 1960s. A muse to photographer David Bailey, she was described by _Vogue_ editor-in-chief Diana Vreeland as "the most contemporary girl I know." She appeared on the cover of British _Vogue_ and _Show_ magazine in 1964. That same year, journalist Tom Wolfe heralded her as the "Girl of the Year," recognizing her as a symbol of the era's emerging youth culture and changing social landscape. Holzer starred in several of Warhol's underground films, including _Soap Opera_ (1964), _Couch_ (1964), _Batman Dracula_ (1964), and _Camp_ (1965). In 1966, _[Women's Wear Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's\_Wear\_Daily "Women's Wear Daily")_ named her one of New York's "fashion revolutionaries." She later established a successful career as a real estate investor in Palm Beach.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Jane Brukenfeld was born and raised in Palm Beach, Florida, the daughter of real estate and insurance investor Carl Brukenfeld (1906–1962).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:3-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:13-2) Her family's wealth derived from extensive real estate holdings throughout Florida, including numerous properties in Palm Beach and more than eight miles of oceanfront land on Merritt Island, now part of Cape Canaveral.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:3-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:1-3) Her father and grandfather, Morris Brukenfeld, were active in the development of Worth Avenue, helping to found the Worth Avenue Merchants Association and constructing several commercial buildings along the avenue.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:13-2) In 1951, her father established the Brukenfeld Family Foundation, a philanthropic organization.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-4)
She grew up in a Jewish household and attended Palm Beach High School for a year before transferring to Cherry Lawn School in Darien, Connecticut.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965215-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:12-6)
Brukenfeld was admitted to Finch Junior College in Manhattan, but she spent most of her time at dancing at El Morocco, and "flunked out of college on purpose to become a model."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965216-7)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:1-3)

Before her marriage, Jane Holzer modeled professionally under her maiden name, Jane Brukenfeld, in New York and Paris.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8) She was scheduled to walk in Hubert de Givenchy's Paris couture presentations but left the city shortly before the shows to marry Leonard Holzer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8)
In April 1963, the British magazine _Tatler and Bystander_ profiled Holzer in its series of beauty in fashion, describing her as an elegant young American socialite whose style was reminiscent of Grace Kelly.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8) The magazine highlighted her Paris wardrobe, her preference for the designs of Coco Chanel, Balenciaga, Yves Saint Laurent, and Hermès, and suggested that she was a future contender for the International Best Dressed List.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8) It also compared her appearance to that of Italian actress Monica Vitti.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8)
Later in 1963, Holzer's modeling career gained momentum after she traveled to London, where she was photographed by David Bailey.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965216-7) In a 1964 interview with Tom Wolfe, Holzer credited Bailey with launching her career, saying, "Bailey created four girls that summer. He created Jean Shrimpton, he created me, he created Angela Howard and Susan Murray. There's no photographer like that in America. Avedon hasn’t done that for a girl, Penn hasn't, and Bailey created four girls in one summer. He did some pictures of me for the English _Vogue_, and that was all it took."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965216-7)

**Getting your Trinity Audio player ready…**
Dina Merrill, an heiress turned actress who starred in classic movies such as 1960’s “BUtterfield 8” and 1963’s “The Courtship of Eddie’s Father” died Monday in East Hampton, New York, the New York Timesreported. She was 93.
Her death was confirmed by , Stanley H. Rumbough, who said she suffered from Lewy Body dementia.
The daughter of Wall Street giant E.F. Hutton and cereal scion Marjorie Merriweather Post, Merrill grew up surrounded by wealth.
According to the Times, she spent up to half of each year as a child on the family’s giant yacht, the Sea Cloud, and the other half on a 115-room estate in Mar-a-Lago, Florida, that was renovated into a private club after its purchase by future U.S. President Donald Trump in 1985. (Ivanka Trump shared the same childhood bedroom suite, the Times wrote.)

# Dina Merrill, Heiress Turned Actress Who Grew Up in Trump’s Future Mar-a-Lago Estate, Dies at 93
## Share on Social Media
Merrill defied her father’s wishes by becoming an actress, making her Broadway debut in 1945’s “The Mermaids Singing.” But she was 34 by the time she got her first movie role — in the 1957 Katharine Hepburn-Spencer Tracy comedy “The Desk Set” — because she took time out to raise three children with her first husband, the Colgate-Palmolive heir Stanley M. Rumbough Jr. (The couple divorced in 1966.)
But then she landed a series of high-profile roles in Hollywood, as the daughter of a Wall Street banker in 1959’s “What Makes Sammy Run” and as jilted wives in “BUtterfield 8” opposite Liz Taylor and “The Courtship of Eddie’s Father” with Glenn Ford and Shirley Jones.
Other noteworthy roles included 1959’s “Operation Petticoat,” 1960’s “The Sundowners,” 1961’s “the Young Savages” and Robert Altman’s 1992 Hollywood comedy “The Player.”
In 1966, Merrill married actor Cliff Robertson — though they divorced in 1989. She then married actor turned film producer Ted Hartley.
Merrill was a moderate Republican who served as vice chair for the Republican Pro-Choice Coalition and vice president of the New York Mission Society, the Times wrote. She also contributed heavily to the Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation.

**Jane Holzer** (née**Brukenfeld**; born October 23, 1940), also known as **Baby Jane**, is an American model, actress, art collector, and real estate investor. She rose to prominence during the 1960s as Pop artist Andy Warhol's first "Superstar."
Known for her voluminous teased blonde hair, Holzer emerged as an influential figure in the international fashion scene and became emblematic of a new form of media celebrity in the 1960s. A muse to photographer David Bailey, she was described by _Vogue_ editor-in-chief Diana Vreeland as "the most contemporary girl I know." She appeared on the cover of British _Vogue_ and _Show_ magazine in 1964. That same year, journalist Tom Wolfe heralded her as the "Girl of the Year," recognizing her as a symbol of the era's emerging youth culture and changing social landscape. Holzer starred in several of Warhol's underground films, including _Soap Opera_ (1964), _Couch_ (1964), _Batman Dracula_ (1964), and _Camp_ (1965). In 1966, _[Women's Wear Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's\_Wear\_Daily "Women's Wear Daily")_ named her one of New York's "fashion revolutionaries." She later established a successful career as a real estate investor in Palm Beach.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Jane Brukenfeld was born and raised in Palm Beach, Florida, the daughter of real estate and insurance investor Carl Brukenfeld (1906–1962).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:3-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:13-2) Her family's wealth derived from extensive real estate holdings throughout Florida, including numerous properties in Palm Beach and more than eight miles of oceanfront land on Merritt Island, now part of Cape Canaveral.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:3-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:1-3) Her father and grandfather, Morris Brukenfeld, were active in the development of Worth Avenue, helping to found the Worth Avenue Merchants Association and constructing several commercial buildings along the avenue.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:13-2) In 1951, her father established the Brukenfeld Family Foundation, a philanthropic organization.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-4)
She grew up in a Jewish household and attended Palm Beach High School for a year before transferring to Cherry Lawn School in Darien, Connecticut.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965215-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:12-6)
Brukenfeld was admitted to Finch Junior College in Manhattan, but she spent most of her time at dancing at El Morocco, and "flunked out of college on purpose to become a model."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965216-7)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:1-3)

## Early life and education
### Early modeling career
[edit]
Before her marriage, Jane Holzer modeled professionally under her maiden name, Jane Brukenfeld, in New York and Paris.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8) She was scheduled to walk in Hubert de Givenchy's Paris couture presentations but left the city shortly before the shows to marry Leonard Holzer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8)
In April 1963, the British magazine _Tatler and Bystander_ profiled Holzer in its series of beauty in fashion, describing her as an elegant young American socialite whose style was reminiscent of Grace Kelly.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8) The magazine highlighted her Paris wardrobe, her preference for the designs of Coco Chanel, Balenciaga, Yves Saint Laurent, and Hermès, and suggested that she was a future contender for the International Best Dressed List.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8) It also compared her appearance to that of Italian actress Monica Vitti.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:14-8)
Later in 1963, Holzer's modeling career gained momentum after she traveled to London, where she was photographed by David Bailey.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965216-7) In a 1964 interview with Tom Wolfe, Holzer credited Bailey with launching her career, saying, "Bailey created four girls that summer. He created Jean Shrimpton, he created me, he created Angela Howard and Susan Murray. There's no photographer like that in America. Avedon hasn’t done that for a girl, Penn hasn't, and Bailey created four girls in one summer. He did some pictures of me for the English _Vogue_, and that was all it took."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWolfe1965216-7)

## Early life and education
### Early modeling career
The earliest known published use of her nickname "Baby Jane" appeared in October 1963, when society columnist Cholly Knickerbocker reported on Holzer's shopping trip in Paris.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-9) The sobriquet remained associated with her throughout her career.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:20-10) According to Holzer, the nickname had been jokingly given to her by _[Women's Wear Daily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's\_Wear\_Daily "Women's Wear Daily")_ columnist Carol Bjorkman as a reference to the 1962 film _What Ever Happened to Baby Jane?_[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:20-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:19-11) Although Bjorkman did not refer to Holzer as "Baby Jane" in her "Carol Says" column until October 1964, Holzer credited her with originating the nickname.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:20-10)

## Early life and education
### Mainstream acting and music career
[edit]
In 1965, Holzer began pursuing a mainstream entertainment career beyond Warhol's underground films.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:22-37) She studied acting with Sanford Meisner in New York and appeared as a guide to New York's jet-set lifestyle on the ABC television program _The Wild, Wild East_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:22-37) She also taped a television special starring Frank Sinatra and [Sammy Davis Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Davis_Jr. "Sammy Davis Jr.") for CBS.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:22-37) Reflecting on her transition to mainstream acting, Holzer remarked, "Up to now, my acting roles have been so off off-Broadway, they've been practically underground." She acknowledged that "My biggest problem in Hollywood has been convincing people I'm not a kook," adding, "But I have a mind, and I want to use it."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Holzer#cite_note-:22-37)

Dina Merrill, an heiress turned actress who starred in classic movies such as 1960’s “BUtterfield 8” and 1963’s “The Courtship of Eddie’s Father” died Monday in East Hampton, New York, the New York Timesreported. She was 93.
Her death was confirmed by , Stanley H. Rumbough, who said she suffered from Lewy Body dementia.
The daughter of Wall Street giant E.F. Hutton and cereal scion Marjorie Merriweather Post, Merrill grew up surrounded by wealth.
According to the Times, she spent up to half of each year as a child on the family’s giant yacht, the Sea Cloud, and the other half on a 115-room estate in Mar-a-Lago, Florida, that was renovated into a private club after its purchase by future U.S. President Donald Trump in 1985. (Ivanka Trump shared the same childhood bedroom suite, the Times wrote.)

# Dina Merrill, Heiress Turned Actress Who Grew Up in Trump’s Future Mar-a-Lago Estate, Dies at 93
## Share on Social Media
Merrill defied her father’s wishes by becoming an actress, making her Broadway debut in 1945’s “The Mermaids Singing.” But she was 34 by the time she got her first movie role — in the 1957 Katharine Hepburn-Spencer Tracy comedy “The Desk Set” — because she took time out to raise three children with her first husband, the Colgate-Palmolive heir Stanley M. Rumbough Jr. (The couple divorced in 1966.)
But then she landed a series of high-profile roles in Hollywood, as the daughter of a Wall Street banker in 1959’s “What Makes Sammy Run” and as jilted wives in “BUtterfield 8” opposite Liz Taylor and “The Courtship of Eddie’s Father” with Glenn Ford and Shirley Jones.
Other noteworthy roles included 1959’s “Operation Petticoat,” 1960’s “The Sundowners,” 1961’s “the Young Savages” and Robert Altman’s 1992 Hollywood comedy “The Player.”
In 1966, Merrill married actor Cliff Robertson — though they divorced in 1989. She then married actor turned film producer Ted Hartley.
Merrill was a moderate Republican who served as vice chair for the Republican Pro-Choice Coalition and vice president of the New York Mission Society, the Times wrote. She also contributed heavily to the Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation.

**Douglas Joseph Cardinal**OCFRAIC (born 7 March 1934) is a Canadian architect based in Ottawa, Ontario. His architecture is influenced by his Indigenous heritage, as well as European Expressionist architecture.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-CE-1) Cardinal designed the Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau, Quebec, and the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, DC.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:8-2)
Born in Calgary, Alberta, to parents Joseph and Frances Cardinal, Douglas Cardinal is the oldest of eight children.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-3) He is a member of the Siksika Nation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-4) His father was of Siksika (Blackfoot), French, and Ojibwe heritage, while his mother was of German, French and Mohawk/Métis descent.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-NYT-5)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-CE-1) His mother worked as a nurse and was well educated.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-6)

Cardinal's parents met in 1926. Despite the limited rights of women in the early 20th century, which discouraged women's education, the matrilineal culture of Cardinal's father's tribe accepted Cardinal's mother.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7) These cultural ideas shaped Cardinal's upbringing and affected his worldview and relationship with his heritage. He has recalled that his mother told him at a young age, "You’re going to be an architect."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7)
Cardinal grew up just a few miles outside the small city of Red Deer, Alberta. He attended St. Joseph's Convent Catholic, a boarding school designed for rural children who wanted to continue their education beyond Grade 8—the highest level offered by most one-room country schools at the time. He completed high school there. The school was run by the Daughters of Wisdom who were highly regarded for teaching both Catholic and Protestant students.
Like many boarders, Cardinal was introduced to the arts and culture by the Sisters. He later credited the school with having a profound influence on his development. Exposure to traditional architecture and its cultural significance inspired Cardinal to design spaces similar to churches and basilicas.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:1-8)
In 1953, he started studying architecture at the University of British Columbia (UBC) but was forced to leave two years later due to his radical ideas. Cardinal's architectural approach was to create buildings that responded to nature, which did not align with the ideas of modernism that were prominent in the 1950s.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:1-8)
In his third year of studies, he was told by the director of UBC that he had the "wrong background" for the program and the profession. Cardinal left UBC and returned to Red Deer to start working at local architectural firms as a draftsman. In response to anti-Indigenous racism at the time, Cardinal eventually left Canada for Arizona and Mexico, and later settled in Texas.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:1-8)

He attended the University of Texas at Austin, from which he graduated with a degree in architecture in 1963. He also studied cultural anthropology.
Cardinal's philosophy was inspired by architect Rudolph Steiner, who he studied at the University of Texas. Steiner's work led Cardinal to study anthropomorphism, which he applied to his work.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7) The idea of anthropomorphism and its concept of responding to human behavior, natural cycles of life, and land tectonics aligned with Cardinal's cultural heritage.
Another inspiration for Cardinal was the work of Frank Lloyd Wright. Cardinal appreciated Wright's way of responding to the landscape with the use of natural materials, such as stone and brick.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:6-9)
Cardinal opened his private practice in 1964. That same year, he was commissioned to design [St. Mary's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary's_Church,_Red_Deer "St. Mary's Church, Red Deer") in Red Deer, Alberta.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-10) Construction was completed in 1968. It has since been recognized as a prominent example in the history of Canadian architecture. In 2007, the church was featured on a Canada Post stamp series featuring four Canadian architects to commemorate the centennial of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada (RAIC).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-11)
Beginning with his work at St. Mary's, Cardinal was one of the first North American architects to use computers to assist in the design process. Cardinal used 3D design programs to lay out the exact dimensions of buildings and help shape his curvilinear designs to the landscape around them.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-12)

In 1993, he was hired by the Smithsonian Institution as the Primary Design Architect for the National Museum of the American Indian (NMAI). The NMAI is currently situated on the National Mall in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), and is directly across from the Capitol of the United States of America. After contractual disputes, Cardinal was removed from the project in 1998 before it was completed, but he continued to provide input into the building's design.
In 2008, his firm was hired by the Kirkland Foundation to design a museum/convention centre in Union City, Tennessee. The Discovery Park of America was intended to be a unique structure housing a multilevel museum, with artifacts from across the nation, as well as large mixed-use community spaces. However, in early 2009, the firm's contract was terminated and all construction activity was halted.

### Architectural style and philosophy
[edit]
Throughout his early years, Cardinal dealt with racism and pressure to conform to mainstream architectural styles. He did not fully embrace his Indigenous heritage until moving to Texas.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:2-13) In 1970s, Cardinal developed his trademark architectural style with organic curvilinear forms. In those years, he also started wearing native clothes and necklaces and became an advocate for Indigenous rights.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:2-13)
Cardinal's connection to his native cultural background influenced his architectural approach. His work explores the relationship between humans, the environment, and the passage of time. Cardinal uses natural materials, organic shapes, and soil and sun studies. As part of his native philosophy, Cardinal's architecture aims to last for seven generations, as opposed to the economically driven and efficient approach of the patriarchal society.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7)
St. Mary's Church in Red Deer, Alberta is Cardinal's first building. Upon his return to Alberta, Cardinal met with Father Werner Merx, who wanted the new church to be innovative and unique. The archbishop of the church, Anthony Jordan, had already appointed another architect for the job, but Merx insisted on hiring Cardinal and realizing his vision. Archbishop Jordan had helped resolve a legal case for Cardinal 10 years earlier and approved Cardinal for the job.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:7-14)
Cardinal start the project in 1967. Despite initial challenges, St. Mary's Church became one of his most iconic designs. The church has 750 seats inside and includes tubular skylights for natural daylight. Its blend of natural organic forms was considered unprecedented for the time.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-15)

### Canadian Museum of History
[edit]
Canadian Museum of History
The Canadian Museum of Civilization, which opened in 1989, is another project that reflects Cardinal's architectural style. The building is located on the banks of the Ottawa River, facing Parliament Hill. Whereas the government buildings in the city centre face away from the river, Cardinal designed the Museum of Civilization building to face the river. He also included a curvilinear facade that wraps around the environment.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-16) The envelope of the building is shaped in an organic form that mimics many shapes commonly found in nature.
In appreciation for the neighboring Parliament buildings, Cardinal used the same limestone material to construct the museum. The museum also engages with its historical context by including totem poles and native murals inside the building.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-17) Cardinal wanted the space inside to feel alive and dynamic.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-18) Former prime minister Pierre Trudeau also encouraged Cardinal to create a museum where people embrace their different backgrounds and learn from each other. Trudeau's idea for a multicultural Canadian society aligned well with Cardinal's vision.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-19)
However, in 1984 the new Brian Mulroney government did not approve Cardinal's design. He lost his team on the project and was not fully paid for his previous work. However, Cardinal was dedicated to completing the building. He eventually finished the museum and it became one of his many fundamental projects.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-20)

### Architectural peers
[edit]
Cardinal was part of a community that included some of Canada's most influential architects, such as Moshe Safdie, Raymond Moriyama, Eberhard Zeidler, Arthur Erickson, Ray Affleck and Ron Thom.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:3-21) Although the members' styles and conceptual vision were different, they all agreed on a shared vision of architecture that conveyed meaning and beauty, rather than the commercial style of the era.
However, Cardinal struggled with personal and financial problems, and consequently he did not receive as much recognition as his peers.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:3-21)
Edmonton Space And Science Centre (1984)

## **2. Frank Gehry**
Frank Gehry, 1929 to 2025, was a Canadian-born American architect. The Pritzker Architecture Prize’s own page for its 1989 laureate records that he was born in Canada in 1929 and became a naturalized United States citizen in 1950. The Canadian Encyclopedia gives his birth name as Goldberg, his birth as 28 February 1929 in Toronto and his death as 5 December 2025 in Santa Monica, California. The Society of Architectural Historians heads its obituary 1929 to 2025 and reproduces statements from SCI-Arc and from a Chicago Tribune tribute putting him at 96 and at his California home when he died. The encyclopedia’s honours list for him runs to twenty-four items and includes Fellow of the American Institute of Architects in 1974, the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1989, the RAIC Gold Medal in 1998, the AIA Gold Medal in 1999, the Royal Gold Medal of the Royal Institute of British Architects in 2000, Companion of the Order of Canada in 2002, the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016 and Canada’s Walk of Fame in 2019. The Canadian Encyclopedia records that he received his Bachelor of Architecture from the University of Southern California in 1954 and studied city planning at the Harvard University Graduate School of Design, and the Pritzker’s own page adds the Harvard Graduate School of Design years as 1956 and 1957, his return to Los Angeles in 1962 to set up his own firm and, much earlier in his career, the Merriweather Post Pavilion of Music in Columbia, Maryland. Ephraim Owen Goldberg as a full birth name runs through the standard accounts, and the sources opened for this entry carry the surname Goldberg and none of the rest.

## **2. Frank Gehry**
Gehry’s major works, as The Canadian Encyclopedia names them, are the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao of 1997, the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles of 2003, the Biomuseo in Panama City of 2013 and the renovation of the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto, which the encyclopedia describes by its bright blue southern facade and its spiralling inner and outer staircases. The encyclopedia prints no year for that renovation. The Pritzker’s own page dates the Gehry Residence at Santa Monica, California to 1978, the house the accounts describe as wrapped in corrugated metal, plywood, glass and chain-link fence, and The Canadian Encyclopedia calls it his own small, pink Santa Monica bungalow; Gehry Partners itself records that he established his practice in Los Angeles in 1962. The Society of Architectural Historians names the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris among his landmark works, and the National Park Service, which took the Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial, the National Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial of the accounts, into the National Park System on 18 September 2020, records it as designed by Frank Gehry, sited just south of the National Mall in Washington, D.C. and dedicated on 17 September 2020.

## **3. Douglas Cardinal**
Douglas Cardinal is a Canadian architect whose buildings turn on curved, flowing masonry forms, and George Brown Polytechnic wrote of him as a practising architect on 23 June 2026 while his own practice site described him as a working master-builder when it was read on 14 September 2026, and The Canadian Encyclopedia places his office in Ottawa. He was born on 7 March 1934 in Calgary, Alberta; his father was of Siksika, or Blackfoot, and European ancestry and his mother of European and Métis ancestry, and his own practice publishes the year and the city without the day. The University of Toronto gave him a Doctor of Laws, honoris causa, on 15 June 2022 and wrote of him then as still designing residential, institutional and industrial buildings and still completing master plans for Indigenous communities. The Canadian Encyclopedia records that the School of Architecture at the University of British Columbia accepted him in 1952 and that he studied there for three years, that the University of Texas School of Architecture at Austin gave him the training he needed, and that he graduated with honours in 1963, a year Indspire’s own laureate page repeats; the encyclopedia reads his mature work as harmonising an attraction to Italian and Spanish baroque buildings with the expressionist arm of European modern architecture, the European Expressionist architecture of the accounts. Indspire records that he practised in Edmonton for eighteen years, establishing an early reputation with St Mary’s Church at Red Deer, Grande Prairie Regional College, the Edmonton Space and Science Centre and the Government Services Centre at Ponoka, and the 1964 the accounts give for the opening of that practice is on none of the pages opened. The Canadian Museum of History, in an interview it publishes, quotes his own words that his father was Anishinaabe and that his mother came from the Blackfoot Reserve, where the encyclopedia gives his father Siksika and European ancestry and his mother European and Métis ancestry, so the two records assign the Blackfoot line to different parents; the Ojibwe and Mohawk lines the received account adds appear by those names on none of the pages opened for this entry.

## **3. Douglas Cardinal**
Cardinal’s Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau, Quebec opened to the public in 1989, seven years after plans for a new building for the National Museum of Man were unveiled. The museum’s own history page carries both dates and names no architect, and the attribution comes from The Canadian Encyclopedia, whose works list prints the building as the Canadian Museum of Civilization in Hull in 1989. The same list carries St Mary’s Church at Red Deer from 1965 to 1968, Grande Prairie Regional College from 1972 to 1976 and Circle of Life Thunderbird House in Winnipeg in 2000, and the University of Toronto separately gives St Mary’s as completed in 1968. The encyclopedia records that in 1993 he was awarded the commission for the National Museum of the American Indian on the National Mall in Washington, DC, a design it calls outstanding, finished after his exclusion from the project and surrounded by controversy, and Indspire’s page, written while the museum was under way, has him working on it; the same encyclopedia list carries the master plan and concept design for expansion of the Saskatchewan Federated Indian College, now the First Nations University of Canada, at Regina in 2003.
The Canadian Encyclopedia’s honours list for Cardinal runs Officer of the Order of Canada in 1990, the Molson Prize for the Arts in 1992, the National Aboriginal Achievement Award in 1995, the RAIC Gold Medal in 1999, the Governor General’s Award in Visual and Media Arts in 2001, the Golden Jubilee Medal in 2002 and the Diamond Jubilee Medal in 2012, and the institute’s own table confirms the 1999 Gold Medal. He is among the most widely honoured Indigenous architects in Canada, which this honours record supports. Indspire’s own laureate page confirms the 1995 award in its architecture category. His own practice’s page states that the International Association of Architects awarded him the declaration of World Master of Contemporary Architecture, a claim that appears there and in the popular accounts of him and on no page of that association opened for this entry.

## **4. Raymond Moriyama**
Raymond Moriyama was a Canadian architect, born on 11 October 1929 in Vancouver, British Columbia, who died on 1 September 2023 at the age of 93. During the Second World War he, his mother and his sisters were sent to an internment camp in western Canada because of their Japanese heritage, which The Canadian Encyclopedia records without naming the camp. The prize the RAIC now calls the RAIC International Prize was established in 2013 as the RAIC Moriyama Prize, on his conviction that remarkable architecture has the power to transform society by promoting the humanistic values of social equality, respect and inclusiveness. The RAIC describes the prize on its own pages as carrying an annual theme. The Canadian Encyclopedia states that it is awarded every two years, and names Moriyama, the RAIC and the RAIC Foundation as its three founders.

**Douglas Joseph Cardinal**OCFRAIC (born 7 March 1934) is a Canadian architect based in Ottawa, Ontario. His architecture is influenced by his Indigenous heritage, as well as European Expressionist architecture.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-CE-1) Cardinal designed the Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau, Quebec, and the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, DC.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:8-2)
Born in Calgary, Alberta, to parents Joseph and Frances Cardinal, Douglas Cardinal is the oldest of eight children.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-3) He is a member of the Siksika Nation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-4) His father was of Siksika (Blackfoot), French, and Ojibwe heritage, while his mother was of German, French and Mohawk/Métis descent.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-NYT-5)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-CE-1) His mother worked as a nurse and was well educated.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-6)

Cardinal's parents met in 1926. Despite the limited rights of women in the early 20th century, which discouraged women's education, the matrilineal culture of Cardinal's father's tribe accepted Cardinal's mother.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7) These cultural ideas shaped Cardinal's upbringing and affected his worldview and relationship with his heritage. He has recalled that his mother told him at a young age, "You’re going to be an architect."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7)
Cardinal grew up just a few miles outside the small city of Red Deer, Alberta. He attended St. Joseph's Convent Catholic, a boarding school designed for rural children who wanted to continue their education beyond Grade 8—the highest level offered by most one-room country schools at the time. He completed high school there. The school was run by the Daughters of Wisdom who were highly regarded for teaching both Catholic and Protestant students.
Like many boarders, Cardinal was introduced to the arts and culture by the Sisters. He later credited the school with having a profound influence on his development. Exposure to traditional architecture and its cultural significance inspired Cardinal to design spaces similar to churches and basilicas.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:1-8)
In 1953, he started studying architecture at the University of British Columbia (UBC) but was forced to leave two years later due to his radical ideas. Cardinal's architectural approach was to create buildings that responded to nature, which did not align with the ideas of modernism that were prominent in the 1950s.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:1-8)
In his third year of studies, he was told by the director of UBC that he had the "wrong background" for the program and the profession. Cardinal left UBC and returned to Red Deer to start working at local architectural firms as a draftsman. In response to anti-Indigenous racism at the time, Cardinal eventually left Canada for Arizona and Mexico, and later settled in Texas.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:1-8)

The Pritzker’s own page dates the Gehry Residence at Santa Monica, California to 1978, the house the accounts describe as wrapped in corrugated metal, plywood, glass and chain-link fence, and The Canadian Encyclopedia calls it his own small, pink Santa Monica bungalow; Gehry Partners itself records that he established his practice in Los Angeles in 1962. The Society of Architectural Historians names the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris among his landmark works, and the National Park Service, which took the Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial, the National Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial of the accounts, into the National Park System on 18 September 2020, records it as designed by Frank Gehry, sited just south of the National Mall in Washington, D.C. and dedicated on 17 September 2020.

## **3. Douglas Cardinal**
Douglas Cardinal is a Canadian architect whose buildings turn on curved, flowing masonry forms, and George Brown Polytechnic wrote of him as a practising architect on 23 June 2026 while his own practice site described him as a working master-builder when it was read on 14 September 2026, and The Canadian Encyclopedia places his office in Ottawa. He was born on 7 March 1934 in Calgary, Alberta; his father was of Siksika, or Blackfoot, and European ancestry and his mother of European and Métis ancestry, and his own practice publishes the year and the city without the day. The University of Toronto gave him a Doctor of Laws, honoris causa, on 15 June 2022 and wrote of him then as still designing residential, institutional and industrial buildings and still completing master plans for Indigenous communities. The Canadian Encyclopedia records that the School of Architecture at the University of British Columbia accepted him in 1952 and that he studied there for three years, that the University of Texas School of Architecture at Austin gave him the training he needed, and that he graduated with honours in 1963, a year Indspire’s own laureate page repeats; the encyclopedia reads his mature work as harmonising an attraction to Italian and Spanish baroque buildings with the expressionist arm of European modern architecture, the European Expressionist architecture of the accounts. Indspire records that he practised in Edmonton for eighteen years, establishing an early reputation with St Mary’s Church at Red Deer, Grande Prairie Regional College, the Edmonton Space and Science Centre and the Government Services Centre at Ponoka, and the 1964 the accounts give for the opening of that practice is on none of the pages opened. The Canadian Museum of History, in an interview it publishes, quotes his own words that his father was Anishinaabe and that his mother came from the Blackfoot Reserve, where the encyclopedia gives his father Siksika and European ancestry and his mother European and Métis ancestry, so the two records assign the Blackfoot line to different parents; the Ojibwe and Mohawk lines the received account adds appear by those names on none of the pages opened for this entry.

## **3. Douglas Cardinal**
Cardinal’s Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau, Quebec opened to the public in 1989, seven years after plans for a new building for the National Museum of Man were unveiled. The museum’s own history page carries both dates and names no architect, and the attribution comes from The Canadian Encyclopedia, whose works list prints the building as the Canadian Museum of Civilization in Hull in 1989. The same list carries St Mary’s Church at Red Deer from 1965 to 1968, Grande Prairie Regional College from 1972 to 1976 and Circle of Life Thunderbird House in Winnipeg in 2000, and the University of Toronto separately gives St Mary’s as completed in 1968. The encyclopedia records that in 1993 he was awarded the commission for the National Museum of the American Indian on the National Mall in Washington, DC, a design it calls outstanding, finished after his exclusion from the project and surrounded by controversy, and Indspire’s page, written while the museum was under way, has him working on it; the same encyclopedia list carries the master plan and concept design for expansion of the Saskatchewan Federated Indian College, now the First Nations University of Canada, at Regina in 2003.
The Canadian Encyclopedia’s honours list for Cardinal runs Officer of the Order of Canada in 1990, the Molson Prize for the Arts in 1992, the National Aboriginal Achievement Award in 1995, the RAIC Gold Medal in 1999, the Governor General’s Award in Visual and Media Arts in 2001, the Golden Jubilee Medal in 2002 and the Diamond Jubilee Medal in 2012, and the institute’s own table confirms the 1999 Gold Medal. He is among the most widely honoured Indigenous architects in Canada, which this honours record supports. Indspire’s own laureate page confirms the 1995 award in its architecture category. His own practice’s page states that the International Association of Architects awarded him the declaration of World Master of Contemporary Architecture, a claim that appears there and in the popular accounts of him and on no page of that association opened for this entry.

## **4. Raymond Moriyama**
Raymond Moriyama was a Canadian architect, born on 11 October 1929 in Vancouver, British Columbia, who died on 1 September 2023 at the age of 93. During the Second World War he, his mother and his sisters were sent to an internment camp in western Canada because of their Japanese heritage, which The Canadian Encyclopedia records without naming the camp. The prize the RAIC now calls the RAIC International Prize was established in 2013 as the RAIC Moriyama Prize, on his conviction that remarkable architecture has the power to transform society by promoting the humanistic values of social equality, respect and inclusiveness. The RAIC describes the prize on its own pages as carrying an annual theme. The Canadian Encyclopedia states that it is awarded every two years, and names Moriyama, the RAIC and the RAIC Foundation as its three founders.

#### Esther Marjorie Hill
Esther Marjorie Hill, architect (born 29 May 1895 in Guelph, ON; died 7 January 1985 in Victoria, BC). Marjorie Hill was a pioneer of women in the profession of architecture in Canada. The first woman to be admitted to the program in architecture at the University of Alberta in 1916 (the program was discontinued in 1939), she transferred to the University of Toronto, becoming the first woman graduate in architecture in Canada. **Douglas Joseph Cardinal**OCFRAIC (born 7 March 1934) is a Canadian architect based in Ottawa, Ontario. His architecture is influenced by his Indigenous heritage, as well as European Expressionist architecture.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-CE-1) Cardinal designed the Canadian Museum of History in Gatineau, Quebec, and the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, DC.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:8-2)
Born in Calgary, Alberta, to parents Joseph and Frances Cardinal, Douglas Cardinal is the oldest of eight children.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-3) He is a member of the Siksika Nation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-4) His father was of Siksika (Blackfoot), French, and Ojibwe heritage, while his mother was of German, French and Mohawk/Métis descent.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-NYT-5)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-CE-1) His mother worked as a nurse and was well educated.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-6)

Cardinal's parents met in 1926. Despite the limited rights of women in the early 20th century, which discouraged women's education, the matrilineal culture of Cardinal's father's tribe accepted Cardinal's mother.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7) These cultural ideas shaped Cardinal's upbringing and affected his worldview and relationship with his heritage. He has recalled that his mother told him at a young age, "You’re going to be an architect."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7)
Cardinal grew up just a few miles outside the small city of Red Deer, Alberta. He attended St. Joseph's Convent Catholic, a boarding school designed for rural children who wanted to continue their education beyond Grade 8—the highest level offered by most one-room country schools at the time. He completed high school there. The school was run by the Daughters of Wisdom who were highly regarded for teaching both Catholic and Protestant students.
Like many boarders, Cardinal was introduced to the arts and culture by the Sisters. He later credited the school with having a profound influence on his development. Exposure to traditional architecture and its cultural significance inspired Cardinal to design spaces similar to churches and basilicas.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:1-8)
In 1953, he started studying architecture at the University of British Columbia (UBC) but was forced to leave two years later due to his radical ideas. Cardinal's architectural approach was to create buildings that responded to nature, which did not align with the ideas of modernism that were prominent in the 1950s.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:1-8)
In his third year of studies, he was told by the director of UBC that he had the "wrong background" for the program and the profession. Cardinal left UBC and returned to Red Deer to start working at local architectural firms as a draftsman. In response to anti-Indigenous racism at the time, Cardinal eventually left Canada for Arizona and Mexico, and later settled in Texas.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:1-8)

He attended the University of Texas at Austin, from which he graduated with a degree in architecture in 1963. He also studied cultural anthropology.
Cardinal's philosophy was inspired by architect Rudolph Steiner, who he studied at the University of Texas. Steiner's work led Cardinal to study anthropomorphism, which he applied to his work.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7) The idea of anthropomorphism and its concept of responding to human behavior, natural cycles of life, and land tectonics aligned with Cardinal's cultural heritage.
Another inspiration for Cardinal was the work of Frank Lloyd Wright. Cardinal appreciated Wright's way of responding to the landscape with the use of natural materials, such as stone and brick.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:6-9)
Cardinal opened his private practice in 1964. That same year, he was commissioned to design [St. Mary's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary's_Church,_Red_Deer "St. Mary's Church, Red Deer") in Red Deer, Alberta.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-10) Construction was completed in 1968. It has since been recognized as a prominent example in the history of Canadian architecture. In 2007, the church was featured on a Canada Post stamp series featuring four Canadian architects to commemorate the centennial of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada (RAIC).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-11)
Beginning with his work at St. Mary's, Cardinal was one of the first North American architects to use computers to assist in the design process. Cardinal used 3D design programs to lay out the exact dimensions of buildings and help shape his curvilinear designs to the landscape around them.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-12)

In 1993, he was hired by the Smithsonian Institution as the Primary Design Architect for the National Museum of the American Indian (NMAI). The NMAI is currently situated on the National Mall in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), and is directly across from the Capitol of the United States of America. After contractual disputes, Cardinal was removed from the project in 1998 before it was completed, but he continued to provide input into the building's design.
In 2008, his firm was hired by the Kirkland Foundation to design a museum/convention centre in Union City, Tennessee. The Discovery Park of America was intended to be a unique structure housing a multilevel museum, with artifacts from across the nation, as well as large mixed-use community spaces. However, in early 2009, the firm's contract was terminated and all construction activity was halted.

### Architectural style and philosophy
[edit]
Throughout his early years, Cardinal dealt with racism and pressure to conform to mainstream architectural styles. He did not fully embrace his Indigenous heritage until moving to Texas.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:2-13) In 1970s, Cardinal developed his trademark architectural style with organic curvilinear forms. In those years, he also started wearing native clothes and necklaces and became an advocate for Indigenous rights.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:2-13)
Cardinal's connection to his native cultural background influenced his architectural approach. His work explores the relationship between humans, the environment, and the passage of time. Cardinal uses natural materials, organic shapes, and soil and sun studies. As part of his native philosophy, Cardinal's architecture aims to last for seven generations, as opposed to the economically driven and efficient approach of the patriarchal society.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:0-7)
St. Mary's Church in Red Deer, Alberta is Cardinal's first building. Upon his return to Alberta, Cardinal met with Father Werner Merx, who wanted the new church to be innovative and unique. The archbishop of the church, Anthony Jordan, had already appointed another architect for the job, but Merx insisted on hiring Cardinal and realizing his vision. Archbishop Jordan had helped resolve a legal case for Cardinal 10 years earlier and approved Cardinal for the job.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:7-14)
Cardinal start the project in 1967. Despite initial challenges, St. Mary's Church became one of his most iconic designs. The church has 750 seats inside and includes tubular skylights for natural daylight. Its blend of natural organic forms was considered unprecedented for the time.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-15)

### Canadian Museum of History
[edit]
Canadian Museum of History
The Canadian Museum of Civilization, which opened in 1989, is another project that reflects Cardinal's architectural style. The building is located on the banks of the Ottawa River, facing Parliament Hill. Whereas the government buildings in the city centre face away from the river, Cardinal designed the Museum of Civilization building to face the river. He also included a curvilinear facade that wraps around the environment.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-16) The envelope of the building is shaped in an organic form that mimics many shapes commonly found in nature.
In appreciation for the neighboring Parliament buildings, Cardinal used the same limestone material to construct the museum. The museum also engages with its historical context by including totem poles and native murals inside the building.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-17) Cardinal wanted the space inside to feel alive and dynamic.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-18) Former prime minister Pierre Trudeau also encouraged Cardinal to create a museum where people embrace their different backgrounds and learn from each other. Trudeau's idea for a multicultural Canadian society aligned well with Cardinal's vision.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-19)
However, in 1984 the new Brian Mulroney government did not approve Cardinal's design. He lost his team on the project and was not fully paid for his previous work. However, Cardinal was dedicated to completing the building. He eventually finished the museum and it became one of his many fundamental projects.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-20)

### Architectural peers
[edit]
Cardinal was part of a community that included some of Canada's most influential architects, such as Moshe Safdie, Raymond Moriyama, Eberhard Zeidler, Arthur Erickson, Ray Affleck and Ron Thom.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:3-21) Although the members' styles and conceptual vision were different, they all agreed on a shared vision of architecture that conveyed meaning and beauty, rather than the commercial style of the era.
However, Cardinal struggled with personal and financial problems, and consequently he did not receive as much recognition as his peers.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Cardinal#cite_note-:3-21)
Edmonton Space And Science Centre (1984)
York Region Administrative Centre (1992)
SmithsonianNational Museum of the American Indian (1993–1998)
First Nations University (2003)
